title: France sinks its own fleet

facts.text: At 4 a.m. on 27 November 1942, German combat groups drove into Toulon. Their mission, Operation Lila, was to seize the French fleet, as Germany took over the rest of Vichy France after the Allied landings in North Africa.

The fleet's commander was Admiral Jean de Laborde, flying his flag in the new battleship Strasbourg. He was hostile to the British and to de Gaulle, and after the landings he had even proposed sailing out to attack the Allies.
On 12 November Admiral Darlan, who had gone over to the Allies in North Africa, called on the fleet to join him. Laborde refused, saying he would move only on a direct order from Marshal Pétain.
Since 11 November standing orders from Vichy's navy minister, Admiral Gabriel Auphan, said the ships must be scuttled rather than fall into foreign hands.

The Germans caught the port admiral, André Marquis, in bed at Fort Lamalgue. German tanks rolled through the main gate of the naval base at 5:25 a.m., and the signal went out to the ships: "Scuttle! Scuttle! Scuttle!"
Crews opened the sea valves and set off demolition charges. When a German officer reached Strasbourg and demanded that Laborde hand her over, the admiral answered that his ship was already sunk.
About 77 vessels were destroyed, among them 3 battleships, 7 cruisers, 15 destroyers and 13 torpedo boats. Twelve Frenchmen were killed and 26 wounded.
Hitler's prize was gone. The Germans took only 39 small ships and a few disarmed destroyers and damaged submarines, and the scuttled ships never fought for either side.

Laborde paid for it after the war. In March 1947 the High Court sentenced him to death for treason, in part for not taking the fleet over to the Allies. The sentence was commuted, and he was pardoned in 1951.

Strasbourg's story did not end that day. The Italians refloated her in 1943, and U.S. bombers sank her again on 18 August 1944 during the liberation of southern France. That is how Navy cameramen found her a few weeks later.

The Scuttling of the French Fleet, extract from John Vader, The Fleet Without a Friend, War History
Heroic End of French Fleet: Scuttled 77 Ships to Avoid Capture by Nazi Germany, War History Online

photoNote: Tier: green. RAF reconnaissance photo, 28 November 1942, the day after: scuttled warships along the piers of Toulon harbor with dense smoke still pouring from burning ships, a cruiser sitting on the bottom at left. Royal Air Force photo, held by the Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division (per Commons; Crown copyright expired), public domain. Commons original 3493 x 2736; saved 1920 x 1504. Scale, not faces: no public domain close photo of Laborde or the crews on the day was found (Bundesarchiv Bild 101I-027-1451-10 and Bild 101I-027-1451-20, CC BY-SA 3.0, are only 800 px). Runner up: U.S. Navy color photo of the wrecked dockyard and sunken destroyers Tartu, Cassard and others, late 1944, 80-G-K-2012, saved as photos/1942-11-27-toulon-b.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:View_of_scuttled_ships_in_Toulon_in_late_1944.jpg).
photoCredit: The scuttled French fleet burning in Toulon harbor, photographed by the Royal Air Force on 28 November 1942. Library of Congress, public domain.

declassified.fact: Five submarines tried to break out instead. Casabianca and Marsouin reached Algiers, Glorieux made Oran, Iris reached Spain and was interned, and Vénus was scuttled at the harbor mouth.

Harbor scenes of the scuttled French Navy, Toulon, 30 August 1944. U.S. Navy film 428-NPC-5262 (burned in timecode).

film.record: 428-NPC-5302, Scenes of waterfront area, Marseilles; French BB (Strasburg), Toulon (NARA 77439)
film.shot_notes: Whole Navy reel, 7 min 10 s, 720 x 480, clean picture (no burned in timecode), silent. 00:05 to 03:35 Marseille waterfront, cathedral and the wrecked transporter bridge: not Toulon, not used. TOULON: 03:36 to 04:08 Strasbourg sitting on the bottom, wide from the water; 04:12 to 04:23 her hull close with boats alongside; 04:32 to 05:08 low angle on her tower and gun turrets (best single image; open here or on the 03:36 wide); 05:12 to 05:24 along her deck; 05:28 to 05:40 another scuttled ship listing beyond a pier; 05:44 to 05:59 wrecked deck plating; 06:00 to 06:32 twin gun mount on a wrecked cruiser; 06:32 to 06:44 a wrecked bridge tower. Camera mostly static, so the cut should move between shots. The brief's reel 428-NPC-5262 (NARA 77430) and 428-NPC-5252 (NARA 77424) carry a burned in timecode across every frame, so they were not uploaded. No film from 27 Nov 1942 itself was found in NARA (German newsreel film is never used).
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Navy, NARA Record Group 428). NARA use status 'Undetermined', the routine flag on 428-NPC reels.
film.date_note: Filmed after Toulon's liberation, NARA date 3 September 1944, not on 27 Nov 1942. Strasbourg had been refloated by the Italians in 1943 and was sunk again by U.S. bombers on 18 August 1944, so the wreck on film is that second sinking; caption it as the scuttled fleet's wrecks at Toulon in 1944.

video.note: U.S. Navy film 428-NPC-5302 (NARA 77439), the wreck of the battleship Strasbourg at Toulon, NARA date 3 September 1944, after her second sinking by U.S. bombers; not film of 27 November 1942. Silent. Cut 19 Nov 2026 from footage/1942-11-27-toulon-strasbourg.mp4: 4:25.0 to 4:29.6 the camera pans along the hull to her tower; 4:58.0 to 5:02.0 low angle on the tower and turrets; 3:38.0 to 3:41.0 Strasbourg on the bottom, wide from the water; 5:24.0 to 5:27.5 along her deck past the guns. The Marseille shots (0:05 to 3:35) are left out. Converted to square pixels. The Instagram and TikTok cover is set to the tower shot at 6.0 s.
